memories.memory_text: I confirmed it was me when the messenger showed me the photo, and I took the envelope—felt its weight, knew it was important before I even opened it.
I read Shawn Hart's words—'They are following you Alex Reeves'—and immediately checked the room behind me with my mirror; then I burned the letter after seeing his signature.

I remember the way Sawyer Reeves casually laid out those pills on the table, and when he said he was on his honeymoon, I felt a sharp annoyance—like something I hadn’t admitted to myself had just been yanked away.
I didn't turn to face him when I spoke—I just held out my valise, letting him take it, and looked at him over my sunglasses with the faintest smile.
I told Sawyer Reeves to leave Cedar Grove District tomorrow—it’s a city for lovers, and he needs to recover, not linger in something that won’t go anywhere.
After locking the door, I whispered to myself that I was doing the right thing—but admitted I wanted him gone, as if confirming it to the silence.

I brought the car to a screeching halt right in front of him, the headlights cutting through the dark, and saw him flinch—kneeling there, stunned—so I opened the door and told him, 'What are you waiting for? Get in.'
I walked up the stairs to the landing and unlocked the door with my key, stepping into the dark Harborview School without hesitation.
I stepped away from Sawyer Reeves into the Northbridge Station, heart beating, and whispered into the phone. When I started to say 'Alexa,' Lane Keaton cut in: 'No names. Not on the phone.'

I opened the Tuscan Cookbook to the lamb recipe, pulled out my red pen, and tapped it beneath the letters in the coded sentence—deciphering the message just as Sawyer Reeves’s eyes opened, though he didn’t speak.
I touched Sawyer Reeves’s shoulder as he slept, my voice quiet but steady when I told him I had to go and not to leave the Northbridge Station.
When he asked when he’d see me again, I said 'Never,' held his gaze for a moment, and then walked away without looking back.
I checked my the red key and picked up my pace—time was slipping, and I couldn’t afford to be late reaching the poolside restaurant.

I fanned myself with the newspaper while scanning the men nearby, watching for anything out of place—the officials by the bar, the tourists with maps—then caught sight of young lovers tangled in the pool, drunk on each other; I turned away.
I saw Sawyer Reeves approaching—clean-cut, in a tailored suit, looking like someone else entirely—and for a moment, I couldn't hide how stunned I was.
I told the waiter not to bring him coffee, and when he defied me by ordering with milk, I asked him if he wanted to be dead—his defiance in that moment felt like a direct challenge.
I told Sawyer Reeves I was leaving him, and when he kept pushing, I threw some Euros on the table and said he and Shawn Hart made a nice couple.
I saw words spelled in salt and pepper on the plate—the message said 'MY VILLA. TONIGHT. 8PM'—but before I could react, the waiter blew it away.
I shot Sawyer Reeves a look and got on the vaporetto without saying a word—he was on his own.
I sketched the sculpture in the Anticollegio, pencil moving carefully across the page, aware this was the first move in a role I’d have to hold perfectly.
I was on the top deck, the wind in my hair, when a hand passed me a drink—I smiled, but didn’t look up. After that, I stopped reporting certain things.

I handed Sawyer Reeves the tape for the the glass photograph, and when our eyes met, there was no act—just quiet understanding. His hands were steady as he helped me fasten it, and for once, I didn’t have to say a word.

When he said I looked like the most beautiful woman on earth, I didn’t react at first—I wasn’t sure I’d heard him right. Then I touched his cheek, not because I planned to, but because it felt like the only real thing I could do.

I was standing in the center of the room, just for a second, and then I saw movement behind me in the doorway—I turned and it was Evan Whitaker, mask off, stepping toward me like he’d been expecting me all along.
I felt the chill as he stepped closer, his voice calm but cutting through the silence like a threat I couldn't escape.
I saw Sawyer Reeves in the doorway, calm, and when he looked at me, I knew he was willing to die for me.
I saw Evan Whitaker turn to me and raise his pistol—point blank. Then Sawyer Reeves threw his body over me. I couldn't see anything after that.

Sawyer Reeves threw himself over me—suddenly, completely—shielding me as glass and splinters rained down. I felt his weight, the impact of gunfire all around, and then silence that lasted long after it was over.

I felt his fingers move under my clothes, and for a second I thought—no, this isn't right—but then he pulled out the the glass photograph, and his voice changed, British now, saying, 'I'm here.' My breath caught. Sawyer Reeves was Shawn Hart.

He said the truth was that he loved me, and I believed him. I saw no lie in his eyes. Then we heard voices below. He moved to the bookshelf, opened a hidden safe in the floor, and pressed his finger to the biometric lock.
I walked toward the exit leaning on Sawyer Reeves's arm, not looking back, even as Morgan Delaney called after me.
When I stopped and turned, I told him there was nothing to talk about — I don’t work for him anymore.
I saw Lane Keaton at the helm—same face, same cold eyes—and in that moment I understood: Sawyer Reeves had orchestrated everything, down to the last detail, to get us out clean.
I didn't take the glass—he offered it, but I stepped into his arms instead, pressing close, feeling the weight of the life behind me dissolve as we kissed under the lights of Cedar Grove District.

memories.memory_text: I reached for her zipper, fumbling at the fabric near her neck, and when the train swayed I pulled too hard—the zipper tore with a sharp sound and I froze, the metal tab in my fingers, realizing I’d ruined her sweater.

The steward called us 'monsieur' and asked if we'd dine together, and before I could correct him, Alex Reeves smiled and said 'the dining car would be lovely'—I just sat there, stunned, watching her play along like we were a real couple.

I remember sitting across from Alex Reeves at that candlelit table, the train moving through the mountains outside the window, the light dimming as the sun set — it felt like we were the only two people in the world.
I told her I was on my honeymoon alone—after my wife left me for a pizza guy. Saying it out loud made it real, sitting there with all those pills on the table.
I joked that I still loved that pizza from the place she left me for—'Bala Pizza' in Rosemont. It felt stupid, but also like the only thing I could say without falling apart.
I stumbled down the train aisle, bumping into people, muttering sorry each time, but I couldn't stop—I had to find Alex Reeves.

I stepped off the train, heart pounding, scanning the crowd until I saw her—Alex Reeves, standing there with her back turned. I hurried over and said I was afraid I’d missed her, that I wanted to know where she was staying… and then she held out her valise without even turning around.
Alex Reeves introduced me as her husband at the hotel desk, and the receptionist looked at me like he couldn't believe she'd be married to someone like me.

I stood on the Pinecrest District, the view spreading out below me, and when Alex Reeves said there was more than enough room for two, I felt something shift—my breath caught, and for a second, I thought she meant us sharing the room as something more than just shelter.
Then she asked if I was all right with the sofa, and I felt my face fall—I had to force myself to smile and say it was fine, perfect even—because I realized I’d misunderstood everything.
I placed my things in the other bathroom—small move, but it felt like stepping further into her world, claiming a sliver of space that wasn’t mine before.
She asked if I’d ever been to Cedar Grove District, and when I shook my head, she said, 'Then we need to go out'—sudden, decisive, like it was settled just like that.

I told Alex Reeves that I'd like to think love is a question of destiny, not chance—said it quietly, almost to myself, after dodging her question about my ex. She looked at me differently after that, like she saw someone else for a second.
I noticed the the red key on her wrist—something about the way it caught the light—and asked her why she was still wearing his the red key. I didn't expect her to take it off and put it on me.
I saw her kick off her shoes and open the doors to the Pinecrest District—something in me just shifted, and I didn’t even think before stepping past the sofa and going after her.
I could get used to this, I said, just before she turned and pressed herself against me—sudden, warm, real—and I held her close, kissing her like I’d been waiting to for too long.
We were kissing on the Pinecrest District, the city quiet below—then later I’d wonder if someone was watching, if the hum I didn’t hear then meant anything at all.

I remember standing there, frozen, after she pulled away and told me to leave Cedar Grove District—her voice so flat, like the fire between us had just been snuffed out. I asked what I did, but she said nothing, just locked herself in the Northbridge Station while I sat down on the sofa with the blankets already laid out like she’d decided this before we even kissed.

I was taking off the the red key Alex Reeves gave me, and when I saw 'Shawn Hart' engraved on the back, I just froze. I didn’t say anything, but I opened my bag, took out my pills, and swallowed a handful without water.
I heard the shower running and couldn't look away—the door was open, and I saw her through the steam, lifting her wet hair as she soaped her neck. I told myself to turn, but I walked forward instead.

I opened the glass door and stepped inside, water soaking my clothes as I lifted her against the glass—her skin was slick, her legs wrapped around me. I remember the urgency in my hands, the way I kissed her, like I couldn't stop even if I should.
I saw the dots on the newspaper, traced the lines through the words—'Tomorrow 11 Caffe Pesaro'—just like solving a puzzle, but this one felt dangerous.

memories.memory_text: I explained Shawn Hart's method of using a fake lawsuit between a casino in Arizona and a shell company in the Cayman Islands to make dirty money appear legal, and noted that the money is not fully legal because the IRS has been cheated.
I presented Shawn Hart’s False Lawsuit scheme during the briefing, explaining how he uses shell companies and fake lawsuits to launder money.

I closed the file and told them no one knows what Shawn Hart looks like now—he vanished after the surgery, just like Carillo did. When Terry Everett challenged me, I kept my voice steady and told them he’d come for her. I could feel the room shift when I said it.

I clicked the slide and her face filled the screen. For a second, I looked up—not just to confirm the image, but because I couldn’t help it. That look must have shown something, though I didn’t mean for it to.
I heard Logan Mercer say she's not alone at the Danieli, and I told the team to maintain surveillance at a distance and not to underestimate Shawn Hart.

I remember asking about the American tourist, and when Remy Delaney said he was just some unlucky guy, I pressed them—Russian hit men don’t chase innocent tourists. If Evan Whitaker’s not our target, he’s still tangled in this.
I shouted 'Go! Go! Go!' as the map locked onto Piazza San Marco, then grabbed my vest and ran down the steps behind Logan Mercer.

I wondered aloud why women are drawn to con men like Shawn Hart—maybe because they adore themselves so completely, it lets the woman feel like a child again, safe in that reflection. I could feel the bitterness in my own voice, and I saw the others shift, unsure how to take it.

After Logan Mercer's phone beeped and we got word she was moving, I pushed myself up from the chair, tired in a way that wasn't just physical. I said, 'Let's follow the children,' and meant every word—not just about the target, but about all of us in this room.
I watched Alex Reeves through the tinted window, barely visible from my position in the cabin—just enough to confirm she was in place.

I saw Sawyer Reeves’s face on the the blue box—clean-cut, in Shawn Hart’s suit—just walking right into the restaurant like he owned the place. My hand froze mid-air, the operation hanging on my next word.
I whispered 'Move off. Move off.' and then snapped at the screen, 'Get rid of him!'—but Sawyer Reeves just sat down, lit a cigarette, and ignored everything we were trying to control.
I ordered Logan Mercer to send Lipetti in to remove Sawyer Reeves, framing it as handling a disruptive civilian—just a rowdy guest needing escorting out.
I saw Sawyer Reeves walking toward Alex Reeves on the the blue box, fifty feet away—reckless, uncoordinated. I said, 'That goddamn fool,' and ordered him thrown in the lagoon.
I lifted the mirror off the wall and set it on the floor, revealing nothing but a plain surface behind it—no observation room, no audience, just silence.
When Sawyer Reeves said he wasn't Shawn Hart, I told him I already knew—had known since the beginning—watching the certainty drain from his face.

I showed Sawyer Reeves the CID Academy photo from 2002, making him recognize the younger version of me standing as an instructor—then guiding his eyes to Alex Reeves in the second row, watching the moment he realized she was never who he thought she was.

I told Sawyer Reeves we’d been watching him the whole time, and when he threatened to go to the embassy or the press, I stopped him by making it clear that exposing the truth would end Alex Reeves’s career—he understood, and fell silent.
I handed Sawyer Reeves an espresso and said women like Alex Reeves don't come along often—she was stunning, brilliant, the worst combination for someone in our world.
I told Sawyer Reeves she's all I have, and I meant it—Alex Reeves is my only option, even if I can't be sure she'll succeed.
I apologized to Alex Reeves in the hallway, admitting I was on edge because of the operation's failure—something I don't usually let show.
When Alex Reeves asked if Shawn Hart might still have been at the event, I felt a sudden spark—I'd been so focused on the failure that I hadn't considered it. My mind snapped back to possibility.

I strode in and called the team to attention—Remy Delaney, Micah Monroe, Terry Everett, the rest—laid out the plan: Shawn Hart’s villa at eight, no time to waste. When Sawyer Reeves interrupted with unsolicited advice, I shut him down sharply; this operation doesn’t need distractions.

I sat down next to Sawyer Reeves with the International Herald Tribune, letting him see I had it—showing him how Shawn Hart uses the classified ads to stay off the grid. There's no signal to intercept when the message moves through paper.

I heard the sharp, muffled crack of a silenced shot over the radio—then static where the agent’s voice should have been. By the time I processed it, he was already gone, and the perimeter was breached.
I saw the feeds go dark one by one and snapped at the technician—get it back online, stop him—knowing we were losing control.
After everyone started panicking, I shut them down and turned my focus to audio—asked if we still had it, then ordered it turned up when the screens went black.
I silenced the team when they started speculating—Remy Delaney was about to say something, but I cut him off. It was Evan Whitaker’s voice, and I knew we had to stay quiet and wait for Shawn Hart.

I stood there as the slaps echoed, each one sharper than the last, and Alex Reeves’s cries cut through the silence—I told myself we had to wait, that she was my agent and I wouldn’t risk the mission, even as Terry Everett’s voice cracked with urgency.

I felt their eyes on me—Logan Mercer, Terry Everett, Remy Delaney—all holding their weapons, bodies coiled, waiting for my word to move, and then Logan Mercer’s voice broke the tension: 'Where’s Sawyer Reeves?'—and I realized one of my own was already gone.
I gave the order—'Do it'—after her scream faded, the word sharp in the silence, necessary despite the weight of what followed.
I led the team toward the villa, weapons ready, closing in as the perimeter tightened with undercover agents moving into position.
I called out to Alex Reeves, tried to apologize, but she didn’t stop—just turned, told me it was over, and walked out with Sawyer Reeves.
I saw Logan Mercer find a flash drive in the safe. The techs plugged it in and showed account numbers and access codes. The total was 744 million.
